title: Anytime Detection of Strategic Deviations in Multi-Agent Systems
one_liner: Detect when agents stop playing fairly or as expected, by betting against their behavior and watching the bet grow.
lead: When multiple agents interact repeatedly (like traders in a market or robots sharing a workspace), they often settle into predictable patterns. But in real life, behavior drifts. This paper gives a way to spot drift as it happens—without waiting for a fixed amount of data—by treating deviation detection as a repeated betting game. The method works for simple repeated games and complex changing games alike.

paras: In repeated multi-agent games, a simple rule is: agents should play an equilibrium (a stable mix of strategies where no one wants to unilaterally switch). In the real world, agents drift. A trader might break from their usual strategy, a drone in a swarm might stall, a data center might start cheating on latency promises. A naive approach: collect a big batch of data, then run a statistical test saying either 'equilibrium' or 'not equilibrium.' The problem: you have to choose the batch size in advance. If you choose small, noise drowns out the real drift. If you choose large, you waste time before raising an alarm.
No good principled way exists to test on-the-fly: stop whenever the evidence is strong enough, without the risk of false alarms piling up as you keep checking.

callout.html: Detect when agents deviate from equilibrium play as it happens, with real-time statistical guarantees and no fixed sample size.

panels.title: 1. Two agents play repeatedly
panels.caption: Agents interact; each gets a payoff. Expect equilibrium.

panels.title: 2. Payoffs stay as expected
panels.caption: Over time, payoff stays near its expected value. No alarm.

panels.title: 3. Payoffs start to drift down
panels.caption: Agent deviates; payoff drifts below expectation. The bet grows.

panels.title: 4. A betting log rises

panels.title: 5. Alarm when bet exceeds threshold
panels.caption: Bet crosses a safety threshold; raise alarm, decision made, stop.

steps.text: Define what 'correct play' looks like (Nash equilibrium, correlated equilibrium, or a target policy).

steps.b: For each round, compute expected payoff
steps.text: Under the benchmark, what should an agent earn? Write down the prediction.
The agent plays, the game resolves, measure the actual reward.

steps.b: Update a bet (a number that grows or shrinks)
steps.text: If actual payoff falls short, multiply the bet by a factor that encodes how surprising this is. If it matches, keep the bet flat or grow it gently.

steps.b: Raise an alarm when the bet crosses a threshold
steps.text: Pick a safety level in advance. The moment the bet exceeds it, announce 'deviation detected' and stop.

paras: The paper introduces a tool called an e-value: a number that tracks cumulative evidence against the benchmark without committing to a sample size upfront. Instead of gathering N samples then deciding, an e-value lets you peek at the data anytime and stop with a guarantee that false alarms will not pile up.

hidden.name: Cumulative log-likelihood ratio
paras: The paper measures a hidden quantity called the cumulative log-likelihood ratio. In plain terms: at each round, it computes 'how many times more likely is this payoff if the agent is cheating versus if the agent is playing the benchmark?' It multiples these ratios together across all rounds, building up a 'strength of evidence' against equilibrium play.

The method estimates this by watching payoff shortfalls. If the benchmark predicts the agent should earn 60 and earns 30, that is a 50% miss. If this happens repeatedly, the log-ratio compounds. Once the compounded ratio exceeds a safety threshold (say, 20:1 odds against equilibrium), the paper raises an alarm.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger evidence against equilibrium play. Bigger shortfalls multiply the evidence.

reads.html: Think of a jury. Each round, the jury hears a new piece of evidence (a payoff outcome). If the outcome fits equilibrium, the jury stays neutral. If it conflicts, the jury records 'one point against equilibrium.' Once enough points pile up, the jury announces 'guilty of deviation.'

The paper constructs a supermartingale (a running bet that satisfies a no-arbitrage property) such that its expected value stays 1 under the null hypothesis (equilibrium play), but grows exponentially under deviations. Anytime a stopping time occurs (the bet exceeds a threshold), the probability of false alarm is at most the inverse of the threshold.

mechanism.h2: Why betting works as a detector
paras: The core insight: a bet is a way to encode surprise. If you expect a payoff of 60 and it lands on 60, you are not surprised; the bet stays at 1. But if you expect 60 and get 30, you are surprised; multiply the bet by 2 (or higher, depending on how surprising). Do this repeatedly. Under equilibrium play, lucky rounds balance unlucky rounds, so the bet wanders but does not grow on average. Under deviant play, unlucky rounds pile up; the bet climbs. When the bet gets large enough (20, 100, 1000), it is astronomically unlikely to have happened by chance.

The trick is mathematical: once you have chosen your surprise multiplier in advance, the bet itself is a 'fair game' under equilibrium. It can still jump up or down in any single round, but on average it stays put. Only under true deviation does it trend upward. This means you can peek at the bet at any time and still make a sound decision: if it is large, deviation is real; if it is small, keep watching.

stages.s: Observed payoff (actual reward the agent got)
Compare to benchmark (what equilibrium says it should be)
Measure gap (how far short of expectation)
Convert gap to surprise multiplier (bigger gap means bigger multiplier)
Multiply running bet by the multiplier
New bet value; if exceeds threshold, raise alarm

math.h2: The equation that runs the alarm
math.words: The bet at round t is the product of surprise factors from all prior rounds. Each factor encodes the likelihood of the observed payoff under cheating versus under equilibrium.
symbols: the bet value after round t
the bet value after round t-1
a tuning parameter (larger = more sensitive to small gaps)
what the agent actually earned in round t
what the benchmark predicted for round t
the exponential function (turns a small number into a growth multiplier)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Benchmark predicts payoff = 60. Agent earns 60. Gap = 0. Multiplier = exp(0.1 * 0) = exp(0) = 1.0. Bet stays: E_1 = 1.0 * 1.0 = 1.0.
Benchmark predicts payoff = 60. Agent earns 50. Gap = -10. Multiplier = exp(0.1 * -10) = exp(-1) ≈ 0.37. Bet shrinks: E_2 = 1.0 * 0.37 = 0.37.
Benchmark predicts payoff = 60. Agent earns 30. Gap = -30. Multiplier = exp(0.1 * -30) = exp(-3) ≈ 0.05. Bet shrinks hard: E_3 = 0.37 * 0.05 = 0.0185.

Wait, the bet shrinks? Yes; but in the long run, if deviations keep happening, the negative gaps accumulate and the product becomes very small. This is why we flip the sign in the real paper: multiply by exp(-lambda * gap) for gaps below zero, so the bet GROWS when payoffs fall short. Corrected: E_3 = 0.37 * exp(+3) ≈ 0.37 * 20.1 ≈ 7.4. After ten such rounds, E grows to thousands.

math.note: The bet compounds because each round's surprise is multiplied onto the running total, turning small per-round signals into a large cumulative alarm.

bars.h2: Comparison: fixed-sample test versus anytime e-value

charts.title: Old way: fixed-sample test
rows: False alarm rate controlled but only after all samples
charts.note: You must decide how many samples before observing any data. Too few and noise drowns truth. Too many and you wait forever.

charts.title: This paper: anytime e-value
rows: Bet grows as deviation persists; alarm guaranteed sound whenever raised
charts.note: You can stop and decide at any time. If you are wrong, you get caught only once per experiment.

items.html: If the benchmark is incorrect (e.g., Nash equilibrium does not actually hold for the game's rules and payoffs), the method will sound false alarms. The e-value detects deviations from the stated benchmark, not from truth. Choose your benchmark carefully.

If the observed payoff is corrupted by random noise (sensor error, execution variance), the method becomes harder to tune. A weak signal can be drowned. The method still works (it is designed for randomness) but needs more rounds or higher thresholds to be certain.
If you set lambda (the knob that controls how sensitive the method is) too high, tiny accidental misses trigger the alarm. False positives spike. You lose the guarantee.

items.b: Benign drift that is not strategic deviation.
items.html: If agents adapt their play over time (learning, not cheating), the method sees the payoff change and raises an alarm even though no one is breaking the rules. The method detects any deviation from the fixed benchmark, not the intent behind it.

items.b: Done right: set the threshold high and lambda conservatively; re-verify the benchmark matches reality; track many rounds.
items.html: With a carefully chosen benchmark, conservative tuning, and patience for repeated observations, the e-value method gives you sound online detection with no overstated confidence.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simulator for a simple two-player game (like Rock-Paper-Scissors with uneven payoffs, or a coordination game). Program one agent to play Nash equilibrium; program another to deviate (e.g., always favor Rock after round 50). Run the e-value test. Record: how many rounds until the bet crosses the alarm threshold? Vary the deviation severity. Vary the tuning parameter lambda. Measure: does the alarm trigger faster for bigger deviations (because a larger gap in payoffs means a bigger multiplier per round, so the bet climbs faster)? Does a lower lambda cause false alarms on honest equilibrium play (because lowering lambda makes the method more sensitive, raising false positives)?
demo.metric_eq: detection_delay = round number when bet first exceeds threshold; false_alarm_rate = fraction of honest equilibrium trials where bet crossed threshold by accident
demo.closing: Stronger deviations are caught faster because bigger payoff gaps mean bigger multipliers each round, so the bet climbs faster. Honest equilibrium play does not trigger false alarms because ups and downs cancel on average, keeping the bet near 1.
